body: Request manuscripts as **.docx**, not plain text or pasted text. Word files preserve italics, smart quotes, em dashes, and scene breaks; plain-text paste loses them.
Edit in a lossless round-trip (.docx → markdown → .docx or equivalent). Asterisks in the extracted text are the author's italics; verify each one is real emphasis before touching it.

After rendering back, sanity-check that emphasis survived the round-trip: diff the italic spans before and after. Word-processor exports sometimes extend an italic run over the trailing `."` of a sentence—move closing punctuation outside the span.
Deliver a **clean edited file plus a changelog** (before → after list and author queries). The changelog is the review surface; do not rely on tracked changes surviving conversion.
Preserve the author's voice, especially in casual or interior first-person narration. This is a *light* copyedit regime: fix mechanics, don't rewrite. **Keep:**
- Sentence fragments used for rhythm or emphasis. *"Gone. Just like that." / "Or worse."*
- Conversational discourse markers: "Like, sure,…", "I mean", "I guess", "sure".
- Profanity and slang in dialogue and narration (do not soften).
- Coined words and neologisms. Do not "correct" invented vocabulary; record each coinage and its styling on the book's word list and apply it consistently.
- Intentional repetition for effect (e.g., "The same… The same…").
**Fix:** grammar slips, missing/extra words, agreement errors, typos, mistaken homophones, dropped punctuation, inconsistent styling.
When fragment vs. error is ambiguous, preserve if it scans as deliberate; query rather than rewrite.
- Each speaker gets a new paragraph.
- Put a question-and-answer exchange on **separate** paragraphs, even when terse ("You coming?" / "Why do you care?").
- Dialogue tags lowercase after a comma: `she said, "Let's go."` and `"Never," he said.`
- Capitalize the first word of quoted dialogue introduced by a comma: `shrugged and said, "Let's go."`
- Titles of in-world media, songs, apps, filters, and products: *italics*. *Quiet Harbor: Calm Waters for Your Feed*; *Amber Mornings*.

- Sound effects or asides the author types with literal asterisks (e.g. `*gag*`): **keep the literal asterisks**—do not convert to italics. Place sentence punctuation logically (e.g. `(… *gag*.)` with the period inside the parenthesis).
- Emphasis vs. punctuation: trailing `.`/`,`/`"` go *outside* an italic span unless the author clearly intended otherwise.
- Scene breaks: one device per book (blank line, `* * *`, or an ornament), applied consistently; never rely on a page break alone.
- Title/part/chapter openers: keep the author's heading text verbatim; styling is a layout decision, not a copyedit.

col2: Choose notes-bibliography (humanities default) or author-date (sciences/social sciences) per book; never mix within a book
Endnotes by default, numbered consecutively per chapter; footnotes only for short trade books with few notes or when the author's argument depends on them
Superscript numerals after punctuation; one marker per sentence where possible
Sentence case for all heading levels; no terminal period; no more than three levels below chapter title
col3: "Why the model fails" not "Why The Model Fails"

col2: Levels must nest (no A-head jumping to C-head); a level needs at least two siblings or none
Number by chapter (Figure 3.2, Table 3.1); every figure/table is called out in text before it appears
Sentence case, terminal period if a full sentence; source/credit line at the end in parentheses
Refer to chapter, figure, or table number, never to page numbers ("see chapter 4", "see figure 2.1"); lowercase the generic word
Alphabetical by author surname; multiple works by one author chronologically; 3-em dash for repeated author only if the house template supports it
Set off quotations of 100+ words (or 5+ lines) as block quotes; no quotation marks around the block; citation follows in parentheses or a note
Spell out at first use in each chapter with acronym in parentheses; thereafter acronym only; no periods (NASA, GDP); add a list of abbreviations if more than a dozen
Parallel grammatical structure; bulleted for unordered, numbered for sequence; terminal punctuation only if items are full sentences
Set in italics or reduced type, source on its own line preceded by an em dash, no note or bibliography entry required
Index entries lowercase except proper nouns, subentries indented, page ranges with en dash (112–15); glossary alphabetical, term in bold, definition a fragment or one sentence

body: Watch-list of corrections that recur across manuscripts:
- **Hyphenation of compound modifiers:** taped-off, skin-deep, drug-fueled, ivory-colored before a noun; open when predicate or noun ("a sickly sweetness").
- **Possessives:** someone's, others' — check apostrophe placement.
- **its vs. it's:** "its faultless logic" (possessive), not "it's."
- **Frequent misspellings:** angrier not "angier"; desiccated not "dessicated"; putrefying not "putrifying"; hall pass two words.
- **Subject/verb and there was/were:** "there were so many more people."
- **Dropped/duplicated words:** delete false starts ("I was the I couldn't…").
- **Commas before terminal adverbs and parentheticals** ("…, sometimes") — verify each.
- **Missing prepositions** ("step up to the corner").
- **Question marks** on questions phrased as statements, especially in interior monologue.
- **Plurals vs. singular in lists of named things** ("the names of the parts," not "the name of the parts").
- Authorial fragments and run-ons used stylistically.
- Slang, vulgarity, and dialect in dialogue.
- Invented terminology and neologisms (style them per the book's word list).
- Voice-driven comma splices in fast interior passages — light edit only; query the author rather than silently rewriting if meaning is at stake.
- An author's consistent, defensible choice that differs from house style (e.g. spaced ellipses); note it on the book's stylesheet and follow it.
